enrichment.short_title: Whatley and Graham: Stewart benefit fraud guidelines and specimen counts
key_facts: Whatley was convicted on 13 specimen counts of benefit fraud totalling about £3,100 while the Crown's case involved over £90,000 in overpaid sickness and income support.
Cheryl Graham pleaded guilty to ten benefit fraud counts and asked for 471 further offences to be taken into consideration, receiving about £59,000 over ten years.
The Court reviewed Stewart (1987) guidelines on social security fraud sentencing, inflation since 1987, and post-Stewart appellate decisions.
Both appellants challenged sentences as manifestly excessive; Whatley also argued the judge wrongly sentenced on the full £90,000 contrary to Canavan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeals against Crown Court sentences for benefit fraud.
enrichment.outcome: Whatley's total sentence was reduced from 30 months to 12 months concurrent; Graham's from 30 months to 18 months concurrent; Stewart guidelines retained with £10,000 threshold updated to about £20,000 for contested cases.
enrichment.ratio: Stewart benefit fraud guidelines remain good law save for inflation adjustment to about £20,000, and deterrence may properly feature; under Canavan a defendant convicted on specimen counts must be sentenced on the sums in the counts unless other offences are admitted or taken into consideration.
legal_issues: Whether Stewart sentencing guidelines for benefit fraud require revision
Effect of inflation on the £10,000 Stewart threshold
Whether deterrence remains a limited factor in Crown Court benefit fraud cases
Proper approach to sentencing on specimen or sample counts after Canavan

R v Canavan, Kidd and Shaw [1998] 1 Cr App R(S) 79
R v Clark [1998] 2 Cr App R(S) 95

enrichment.short_title: Jones v DPP: drink-driving case stated appeal on hospital specimens
key_facts: Vivian Jones was convicted after a road traffic collision in Ashstead when her blood alcohol exceeded the prescribed limit.
At hospital she could not provide breath because section 7(2) restricts breath specimens to police stations; a blood sample was placed in her handbag.
On case stated appeal she argued no admissible evidence she was the driver, that police should have explained why breath could not be taken, and that she was not supplied with her blood sample.
The magistrates answered all three questions in the affirmative and the Divisional Court dismissed the appeal as without merit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Dorking Magistrates' Court to the Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates were entitled to find the appellant drove, that no explanation for inability to take breath was required in a section 7(2) hospital case, and that placing the blood sample in her handbag satisfied section 15(5).
enrichment.ratio: In a hospital drink-driving case section 7(2) makes inability to take breath a matter of law so no explanation is required; combined section 9 statements and the appellant's own evidence can prove driving; supply of a blood sample may be effected by placing it in the defendant's handbag if the magistrates so find.
legal_issues: Whether admissible evidence proved the appellant was driving
Whether police must explain why a breath specimen cannot be taken in hospital
Whether section 15(5) requires personal handover of the second blood sample part
linked_authorities: Warren v Metropolitan Police Commissioner [1993] AC 319
R v Duffy [1994] RTR 241
R v Wolley [1995] RTR 139

enrichment.short_title: Gabriel v Boyden: amendment of global renovation claim particulars
key_facts: Peter Gabriel claimed excessive costs and defective works after major refurbishment of his former Freemasons' lodge home in London.
Boyden quantity surveyors and SPL design consultants were sued with Jesmonite suppliers and others for a global damages claim after substantial overruns.
The claimant sought to substitute 69-page amended particulars for an 18-page original pleading after standard disclosure ordered at a case management conference.
Defendants objected on limitation, particularity, prolixity, Henderson economic loss and wasted costs grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application for permission to amend particulars of claim by substitution.
enrichment.outcome: Amendment allowed subject to deletions of a late defects table and conceded passages; defendants given leave to amend defences; further information may be ordered before defence amendments.
enrichment.ratio: Where a complex renovation claim cannot be succinctly pleaded, lack of full particularity or some prolixity does not necessarily bar amendment if there is a real prospect of proof; limitation defences are not lost by allowing previously pleaded time-barred claims to remain in amended pleadings.
legal_issues: Whether proposed amendments were statute-barred or a new cause of action
Whether lack of particularity and prolixity warranted refusal
Whether SPL owed a duty to inspect and Jesmonite suppliers owed a collateral duty of care
Whether recovery of investigation and compromise costs against Boyden was bound to fail

enrichment.short_title: Buckley: unreasonable force in defence of girlfriend on appeal
key_facts: Barry Buckley was convicted of common assault after a drink-fuelled street incident in Chester when his girlfriend was surrounded by a group of abusive girls.
Magistrates accepted he acted in defence of his girlfriend but found his single open-handed push to Amy Hales caused bruising and mild whiplash and used unreasonable force.
Prosecution witnesses had alleged punches; the justices preferred the defence account of one forceful push.
On case stated appeal Buckley argued the force was minimal and that suggesting he could have walked away was a misdirection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Chester Magistrates' Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates were entitled to find the push exceeded reasonable self-defence having regard to size, gender, injury and available lesser options.
enrichment.ratio: Even where self-defence is engaged, a fact-finding tribunal may conclude force was unreasonable where a forceful push by a large man to a much smaller victim caused significant injury and less forceful alternatives such as blocking or leading the girlfriend away were available.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates could find unreasonable force despite Palmer v R
Relevance of alternative courses such as leaving the scene
Whether injury evidence supported a finding of significant force
linked_authorities: Palmer v R [1971] AC 814

enrichment.short_title: SoS Defence v PAT: war disability pension late appeal regulations

statutes_considered.title: Child Support, Pensions and Social Security Act 2000

key_facts: Mr Lynch's 1992 war disability pension claim for deafness was rejected in October 1992 but he did not appeal until September 2002, after new six- and twelve-month time limits took effect in April 2001.

The Pensions Appeal Tribunal initially applied a wrong 'reasonable excuse' test; Newman J remitted the matter but the Tribunal again allowed the late appeal using irrelevant fairness and Article 6 reasoning.
Lynch's explanation referred to his wife's illness in 2000 and confusion about the new time limit rather than a prescribed circumstance in regulation 4.
The Secretary of State sought to quash the March 2004 Tribunal decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a Pensions Appeal Tribunal decision allowing a late entitlement appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; Tribunal decision quashed and remitted for fresh hearing on whether regulation 4 prescribed circumstances were satisfied.
enrichment.ratio: Late war pension appeals must be decided strictly under the 2001 Regulations' prescribed circumstances and practicability requirement, not by freestanding fairness or Article 6 concepts; a Tribunal decision influenced by wrong legal analysis or irrelevant considerations is unlawful.
legal_issues: Correct test under the 2001 Late Appeals Regulations
Whether limitation rules involve substantive rights or procedure
Whether ignorance of the new time limit could be an exceptional circumstance
Whether remittal or final dismissal was appropriate

enrichment.short_title: GPN v O2: strike out of ostensible authority to conclude 3G contract
key_facts: GPN claimed a concluded bespoke contract with O2 for acquisition, design and build works on about 1,923 3G cell sites after negotiations through McCreadies quantity surveyors.
No signed contract existed though 15 draft versions were exchanged; O2 issued a 2000 letter of intent subject to agreed terms and formal contract execution.
GPN relied on Mr Lewis of McCreadies having ostensible authority to bind O2 orally in February 2002; an adjudicator later awarded over £5.7 million.
O2 applied to strike out or obtain summary judgment on the ostensible authority head of claim under CPR Parts 3.4 and 24.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court strike-out and summary judgment application on ostensible authority only.
enrichment.outcome: Claim based on ostensible authority struck out and summary judgment granted for O2 on that issue; other authority and estoppel issues reserved for trial.
enrichment.ratio: Engaging a quantity surveyor to negotiate contract terms does not by silence or partial agreement without referral represent that the agent may bind the principal to a concluded contract; strong facts are needed to rebut the presumption that construction professionals lack ostensible authority to accept tenders.
legal_issues: Whether McCreadies' conduct amounted to a representation by O2
Distinction between negotiating terms and concluding a contract
Effect of the letter of intent and unsigned version 15 contract
Whether agent conduct without principal representation can create ostensible authority

enrichment.short_title: Customs v Jacobs: VAT refund on Hopwell Hall residential conversion
key_facts: Ivor Jacobs converted Hopwell Hall, formerly a residential special school, into a substantial private residence and sought a section 35 VAT refund on building materials and services.
The building had mixed prior uses including boys' dormitories, classrooms and a headmaster's flat; Jacobs also created three new staff flats on conversion.
The VAT Tribunal wrongly treated the whole building as non-residential and held note 9 inapplicable to a whole-building conversion.
Following Blom-Cooper in the Court of Appeal, note 9 applies where a mixed-use building already contained residential parts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 from the VAT and Duties Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Jacobs may recover VAT referable to conversion of previously non-residential parts but not parts previously used as relevant residential accommodation or the headmaster's dwelling.
enrichment.ratio: Section 35 refunds for residential conversion of a mixed-use building are constrained by Group 5 note 9 unless additional dwellings are created; VAT on conversion of parts already used for a relevant residential purpose or as a dwelling is not recoverable.
legal_issues: Whether Hopwell Hall as a whole was non-residential before conversion
Application of note 9 to whole-building conversions after Blom-Cooper
Whether new staff flats were additional dwellings enabling partial recovery
Allocation of VAT between residential and non-residential parts
linked_authorities: Customs and Excise Commissioners v Blom-Cooper [2002] STC 1061
Customs and Excise Commissioners v Blom-Cooper [2003] STC 669

enrichment.short_title: Welsh Water v Carmarthen: tort claims and section 29(5) acknowledgment
key_facts: Piling works in 1995 penetrated Welsh Water's public sewer in Upper Robinson Street, Llanelli; liability was conceded by Carmarthen's solicitors in April 2000.
Welsh Water did not issue proceedings until February 2004, after the primary limitation period expired, relying on section 29(5)(a) acknowledgment.
Carmarthen later denied liability asserting the claim was time-barred despite years of negotiations over remedial works and quantum.
The unquantified claim sought costs of unspecified remedial works for negligence and nuisance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of preliminary issue whether the claim was statute-barred.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed as barred by section 2; tort damages claims fall outside section 29(5)(a) and Welsh Water's claim was not a liquidated pecuniary claim even on liability admission.
enrichment.ratio: Section 29(5)(a) applies to debts and other liquidated pecuniary claims with affinity to contract, not claims for unliquidated tort damages; a bare acknowledgment of liability does not revive a negligence or nuisance claim where remedial scope and quantum remain unsettled.
legal_issues: Whether tort damages claims can fall within section 29(5)(a)
Whether Welsh Water's remedial costs claim was a liquidated pecuniary claim
Effect of April 2000 liability concession on limitation
Distinction between liquidated contractual sums and unliquidated tort damages
linked_authorities: Good v Parry [1963] 2 QB 418

Ross v McGrath [2004] EWCA Civ 1054

enrichment.short_title: Lodgepower v Coulthurst: invalid agricultural repair notice service
key_facts: Lodgepower Ltd, assignee of an oral agricultural tenancy of Higher Core Farm, served a repair notice addressed to the executors of deceased trustee Katherine Coulthurst shortly after her death.
The surviving trustee landlord was solicitor Mr Dickson; Mr Fred Coulthurst opened the notice but was neither landlord nor Dickson's agent at the time.
No regulation 12 counter-notice was served and Lodgepower later sued for about £69,500 repair costs.
The county court held service valid under section 93(3) or (5); the Court of Appeal reversed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from a county court liability-only decision on validity of a tenant's repair notice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; notice invalid for failure to serve the landlord or a present agent responsible for management; claim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A tenant's regulation 12 repair notice must be served on the person entitled to receive rents and profits or on a present agent responsible for management under section 93(3); service on a deceased landlord's executors or an erstwhile agent of a former landlord does not suffice, and Egerton does not support a 'most affected person' test.
legal_issues: Who was landlord after death of one trustee landlord
Whether service on Mr Coulthurst was service on Dickson's agent under section 93(3)
Whether section 93(5) permitted service on the original landlord's former agent
Applicability of Egerton v Rutter to repair notices
linked_authorities: Egerton v Rutter [1951] 1 KB 472
Wilbraham v Colclough [1952] 1 All ER 979

enrichment.short_title: Bartram: section 37(3) hospital order and reopening under section 142
key_facts: Mr Bartram, suffering paranoid schizophrenia and not taking medication, stabbed and killed his dog believing it harboured an evil spirit.
Magistrates found he did the act charged under section 37(3) and remitted him to hospital, wrongly describing the order as an interim section 38 hospital order.
Psychiatric reports in August 2003 showed illness controlled by medication but ongoing schizophrenia; the district judge wrongly concluded section 37 was unavailable and ordered a normal trial.
Bartram had no defence to the absolute liability animal cruelty charge absent insanity, which was unavailable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a district judge's order requiring plea and trial after a section 37(3) finding.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; district judge's order set aside and the court directed to dispose of the case under section 37 by hospital or guardianship order; section 142 is the proper route to reopen such orders.
enrichment.ratio: Section 37(3) allows a hospital or guardianship order without conviction where the accused did the act and mental disorder criteria are met; a section 37(3) order is not a conviction and may be varied or rescinded under section 142 where justice requires, not by reverting to trial without using that power.
legal_issues: Whether section 37 remained available when symptoms were controlled by medication
Availability of guardianship as an alternative to hospital order
Whether the district judge could require trial without using section 142
Effect of section 37(3) orders under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act
linked_authorities: R v Thames Magistrates Court, ex parte Ramadan [1999] 1 Cr App R 386

confidence.notes: Statutory powers, psychiatric evidence and quashing order are all clearly explained.
